title: Listening practice: Directions, a story and a math strategy
description: Three recordings: a teacher's directions for a group activity, a narrated story about a school year, and a teacher explaining a percent strategy.

stimuli.title: Listen: Directions for a group activity

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Okay, scientists, listen carefully, because I'm going to explain the setup now. Today your group is testing how much water three different paper towels can hold back. Each group has three towels, a measuring cup, and a tray.

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: First, cut each towel into a square that's ten centimeters on each side. Second, hold one square over the tray and slowly pour fifty milliliters of water onto it. Third, wait until it stops dripping. Then pour the water from the tray into the measuring cup and read the amount. The towel that lets the least water through absorbed the most. Last, write each result in your table before you test the next towel. One more thing. Towels soak up water because water moves into the tiny spaces between the paper fibers. Scientists call that capillary action.

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Do we all pour at the same time?

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: No. One person pours, one person reads the cup, and one person records. Switch jobs with every new towel.

stimuli.title: Listen: A story about a school year

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text: When Amara walked into her new school in October, she felt like everyone already knew where to go except her. During the first week, she left her notebook on the bus, and she was too embarrassed to tell anyone that she had lost it. So she quietly borrowed paper from Lucía, the girl at the next desk. Lucía didn't say a word about it, but the next morning Amara's notebook was lying on her desk with a note taped to the cover. It said, "The driver found this. Lost things go to the office first." Amara hadn't even known there was an office for lost things. At lunch, she thanked Lucía, who smiled and admitted that she had gone to the office herself, because the same thing had happened to her last year. After that, the two girls sat together every day. By December, Amara was the one explaining to new students where the office was.

stimuli.title: Listen: A math strategy

turns.speaker: Teacher
turns.text: Let me show you a mental math strategy. Suppose a store takes fifteen percent off a jacket that costs forty-eight dollars, and you want to know how much you'll save. Don't panic! First, find ten percent, because that's easy: you just move the decimal point one place to the left. So ten percent of forty-eight dollars is four dollars and eighty cents. Next, find five percent, which is half of ten percent. Half of four dollars and eighty cents is two dollars and forty cents. Finally, add the two parts together: four dollars and eighty cents plus two dollars and forty cents is seven dollars and twenty cents. Why does this work? Because fifteen percent is the same as ten percent plus five percent. We just broke one hard problem into two easy ones.

items.stem: Put the steps in the order the teacher gives them.

items.text: Cut each towel into a square
Write each result in the table

items.explanation: The teacher says first cut each towel into a square, second slowly pour the water onto it, third wait until it stops dripping, and last write each result in the table.

support.clue: Listen for the signal words first, second, third, and last. Each one starts a new step.
support.model: Mentor example (a different task). "First, wash the apples. Second, slice them into thin pieces. Third, spread them on a plate. Last, add a little honey." The signal words keep the steps in order. Listen for the signal words in the directions and order the steps the same way.

items.stem: How does the teacher want the group to share the work?

options.text: Everyone pours the same towel at the same time.
One student pours, one reads the cup, and one records.
The teacher pours the water for each group.
One student does every job while the others watch.

distractors.a: A student asks this, and the teacher answers no.
distractors.c: The teacher gives the directions, but the students do the pouring.
distractors.d: Each person has one job, and the group switches jobs with every new towel. One student does not do every job.

items.explanation: The teacher says one person pours, one person reads the cup, and one person records, and the group switches jobs with every new towel.

support.clue: Listen to the student's question near the end and to the first word of the teacher's answer.
support.frame: In each group, one person ______, another person ______, and the third person ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "In our band, one student plays the drum, one plays the flute, and one sings." The speaker names each person's job in a list. Listen for a list of jobs in the directions and say it the same way.

misconceptions.c: assumes the teacher does the work
misconceptions.d: assumes one person does all the work

items.stem: According to the teacher, what explains the way paper towels soak up water?

options.text: The towels are cut into ten-centimeter squares.
Water is poured slowly onto the towel.
Water moves into tiny spaces between the fibers.
The tray pulls the water out of the towel.

distractors.a: The square size is a setup step, not the scientific reason.
distractors.b: Pouring slowly is a direction for the activity, not why paper soaks up water.
distractors.d: The tray only catches water that drips through; it does not pull water out.

items.explanation: Near the end of her first speech, the teacher says towels soak up water because water moves into the tiny spaces between the paper fibers, which is called capillary action.

support.clue: Listen near the end of the teacher's first speech, after the words "One more thing." Notice the word because.
support.frame: Paper towels soak up water because the water ______ ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different topic). "A mirror fogs up because water vapor in your breath cools into tiny drops on the cold glass." The word because connects a result to its reason. Listen for the reason after because in the talk and choose the matching sentence.

facts: Paper towels absorb water because water moves into the tiny spaces between the paper fibers (capillary action).

misconceptions.a: confuses a setup step with a reason
misconceptions.b: confuses a setup step with a reason
misconceptions.d: reverses the direction of the water

items.stem: Put the events of the story in order.

items.text: Amara found her notebook with a note
Amara and Lucía sat together every day
Amara left her notebook on the bus

items.explanation: Amara lost the notebook on the bus, borrowed paper from Lucía, found the notebook the next morning, thanked Lucía at lunch, and then sat with Lucía every day.

support.clue: Listen for the words that tell time: during the first week, so, the next morning, at lunch, and after that. They show the order.
support.frame: First, ______. Then ______. Next, ______. After that, ______. At the end, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "Kenji missed the first art club meeting. Then he borrowed a friend's sketchbook. The next day he joined the group, and by Friday he had finished his first drawing." Time words show the order. Listen for the time words in the story and order the events the same way.

items.stem: Why didn't Amara tell anyone that she lost her notebook?

options.text: She was too embarrassed.
She already knew where the office was.
Lucía told her to stay quiet.
She was afraid Lucía would be angry.

distractors.b: The narrator says Amara had not known there was an office for lost things.
distractors.c: Lucía never tells Amara anything; she quietly helps her.
distractors.d: Amara borrows paper from Lucía, and nothing suggests she fears her.

items.explanation: The narrator says Amara was too embarrassed to tell anyone that she had lost her notebook.

support.clue: Listen to what the narrator says Amara felt right before she borrowed paper.
support.frame: Amara didn't tell anyone because she felt ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "Tariq didn't raise his hand because he felt nervous about speaking in front of the class." The speaker joins a feeling to an action. Find the feeling that explains Amara's action.

misconceptions.c: adds an event that did not happen

items.stem: What does the ending of the story suggest about Amara?

options.text: She still felt that everyone knew more than she did.
She wanted to change to a different school.
She decided to stop riding the bus.
She learned to help others as Lucía helped her.

distractors.a: By December she is the one explaining things to new students.
distractors.b: Nothing suggests she wants to leave; she makes a friend and settles in.
distractors.c: The story never says she stopped riding the bus.

items.explanation: Lucía helped Amara quietly, and by December Amara is explaining to new students where the office is, so she has learned to help others too.

support.clue: Compare the way Amara felt in October with what the narrator says she is doing by December.
support.frame: At first Amara ______, but by December she ______. This shows that she ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "At first Omar was afraid of the deep end of the pool, but by spring he was teaching his little cousin to swim. This shows that he gained confidence and wanted to help." Compare the beginning and the end to find what changed. Do the same with Amara's story.

misconceptions.b: adds a wish that is not in the story

items.stem: Choose the amounts the teacher finds for the jacket.

dropdown.template: Ten percent of the price is {1}. Half of that, five percent, is {2}.

items.explanation: The teacher says ten percent of forty-eight dollars is four dollars and eighty cents, and five percent, which is half of that, is two dollars and forty cents.

support.clue: Listen for the dollar amounts the teacher says for ten percent and then for five percent.
support.frame: Ten percent of the price is ______. Five percent is half of that, so it is ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different topic). "A recipe uses two cups of flour for one loaf. For half a loaf, use half of the two cups, so one cup." Finding a half means splitting an amount into two equal parts. Listen for the amounts the teacher says and choose the matching ones.

facts: 5% is half of 10%, so 5% of $48 is $2.40.

items.stem: Why does the teacher add ten percent and five percent?

options.text: Because five percent is greater than ten percent.
Because together they make fifteen percent.
Because you always add two percents together.
Because ten percent is the final answer.

distractors.a: Five percent is half of ten percent, so it is smaller.
distractors.c: The teacher adds these two parts only because they make fifteen percent, not because of a rule for every problem.
distractors.d: Ten percent is only one part. The final answer comes after adding both parts.

items.explanation: The teacher says fifteen percent is the same as ten percent plus five percent, so adding the two parts gives the amount for fifteen percent.

support.clue: Listen to the teacher's last two sentences. Notice the words the same as.
support.frame: The teacher adds the two parts because ______ plus ______ is the same as ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "To find 30% of a number, I find 10% three times, because 30% is the same as three tens." The speaker breaks a hard percent into easy parts, then says why the parts fit. Explain the teacher's parts in the same way.

misconceptions.a: reverses the size of the percents
misconceptions.d: confuses the whole with a part
